title: Building an Ansible Automated Compliance Enforcement Framework for AWS Linux Servers
author: BAKRE JAMIU
summary:
Building an Ansible Automated Compliance Enforcement Framework for AWS Linux Servers Introduction Managing the security configuration of Linux servers is an important responsibility in cloud and infrastructure engineering. When you manage multiple servers, checking their configurations manually can become repetitive, time-consuming and difficult to standardize. You might need to inspect SSH authentication settings, verify firewall rules, review privileged accounts, check sensitive file permissions, inspect running services, monitor pending security updates, validate logging and review network security parameters. Doing these checks manually across multiple servers introduces inconsistencies and makes it difficult to maintain reliable compliance evidence. I wanted to approach this problem differently. Instead of repeatedly connecting to individual servers and running commands manually, I decided to build an Ansible Automated Compliance Enforcement framework that could inspect Linux security configurations across multiple AWS EC2 instances, identify compliance gaps, and support controlled remediation. This project was an opportunity to apply practical skills in Ansible, AWS, Linux administration, infrastructure automation and security hardening. In this article, I will walk through the architecture, implementation approach, security checks, troubleshooting process, actual audit findings and lessons I learned while building the project. This is a practical engineering project, not a theoretical demonstration. 1. Project Overview Project: Ansible Automated Compliance Enforcement Author: Jamiu Olatunji Bakre Category: DevOps / Platform Engineering / Infrastructure Automation / Linux Security The objective was to build a reusable automation framework that could: Connect to multiple Ubuntu servers using SSH. Inspect Linux security configurations. Identify security misconfigurations. Evaluate compliance against defined security expectations. Separate security auditing from remediation. Apply approved configuration changes. Re-run audits to validate remediation. Support structured compliance reporting. Infrastructure used The environment consisted of: Component Description Control node Ubuntu running on WSL Managed servers Two Ubuntu AWS EC2 instances Automation framework Ansible Connection method SSH Remote user ubuntu Authentication SSH private key Version control Git Operating environment Linux Screenshot 1 — Project environment Capture your WSL Ubuntu terminal showing your project directory, Ansible version and working environment. 01-project-environment.png 2. Understanding the Architecture I designed the project around an agentless Ansible architecture. The control node runs Ansible and communicates with the managed servers over SSH. There is no requirement to install a separate Ansible agent on each managed server. The control node handles orchestration, while the managed nodes execute the required tasks. Architecture diagram flowchart TB A["Ansible Control Node
Ubuntu on WSL"] B["Ansible Inventory"] C["Compliance Playbook"] D["SSH Authentication"] E["Compliance Audit Role"] F["Compliance Remediation Role"] G["AWS EC2
compliance-server-01"] H["AWS EC2
compliance-server-02"] I["Security Findings"] J["Post-Remediation Audit"] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> G D --> H C --> E C --> F E --> G E --> H G --> I H --> I F --> G F --> H F --> J J --> I How the architecture works 1. Ansible control node This is the machine from which I execute Ansible commands and playbooks. My control node runs Ubuntu under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). 2. Inventory The inventory tells Ansible which servers to manage and how to connect to them. 3. SSH authentication Ansible establishes remote connections using SSH private-key authentication. 4. Managed nodes These are the two Ubuntu EC2 instances receiving the audit and remediation tasks. 5. Compliance playbook The central playbook coordinates the execution process. 6. Audit and remediation roles The audit role checks the security configuration, while the remediation role applies selected changes. 7. Post-remediation verification After remediation, the audit is executed again to determine whether the intended configuration has been achieved. The architecture allows the same automation to be executed against multiple servers without manually connecting to each one. Screenshot 2 — Architecture and AWS infrastructure Capture the AWS EC2 Instances page showing the two managed instances. Hide public IP addresses, account identifiers and other sensitive information. Suggested filename: 02-aws-ec2-infrastructure.png 3. Preparing the Ansible Environment I used Ubuntu on WSL as my Ansible control node. The project was organized inside my Linux home directory. mkdir -p ~/ansible-automated-compliance-enforcement cd ~/ansible-automated-compliance-enforcement I verified the Ansible installation: ansible --version Ansible provides the automation engine used to execute tasks against the managed infrastructure. SSH authentication The managed servers were accessed using an SSH private key. An important troubleshooting issue occurred during the initial connection setup. The inventory referenced a private-key path that did not match the actual location of the key. The investigation identified the intended key location: /home/cloud/.ssh/Your-key.pem I restricted access to the private key: chmod 400 ~/.ssh/your-key-pair.pem This ensures that the private key is not readable or writable by other users. The private key itself is never included in the project repository. Screenshot 3 — Ansible installation Capture the output of ansible --version . Suggested filename: 03-ansible-version.png 4. Configuring the Ansible Inventory Ansible inventory defines the managed infrastructure. I grouped the two EC2 servers under: [compliance_servers] compliance-server-01 ansible_host = YOUR_SERVER_01_IP compliance-server-02 ansible_host = YOUR_SERVER_02_IP [compliance_servers:vars] ansible_user = ubuntu ansible_ssh_private_key_file =/ home / YOUR_USER / . ssh / Your - key . pem The IP addresses above are placeholders. Use your current server addresses when configuring your own environment. The group compliance_servers allows me to execute the same playbook against both managed nodes. For example: ansible compliance_servers -m ping Both servers returned successful Ansible connectivity results during the project. Why inventory groups matter Without inventory groups, managing multiple servers can become difficult as infrastructure grows. By grouping related servers, I can target them together, assign shared variables and reuse the same automation. Screenshot 4 — Inventory configuration Capture the inventory file showing the two host aliases and the inventory group. Blur IP addresses and hide the private-key path if it contains personal information. Suggested filename: 04-ansible-inventory.png 5. Understanding Ansible Connectivity One of the first important tests was confirming that the control node could communicate with both EC2 instances. I executed: ansible compliance_servers -m ping Both managed servers returned successful results. This was an important milestone. The Ansible ping module is different from the traditional Linux ICMP ping command. Instead of simply testing network reachability, the Ansible ping module checks whether Ansible can establish its configured connection and execute a small module successfully. This helped establish that: SSH authentication was working. The inventory was correctly configured. The managed servers were reachable through Ansible. Remote module execution was functioning. 6. Structuring the Project with Reusable Ansible Roles I wanted the project to be maintainable rather than putting every security check into one large playbook. I therefore separated the automation into two major responsibilities: Compliance auditing. Compliance remediation. The audit role inspects the systems. The remediation role applies selected configuration changes. The central playbook coordinates both. The recovered project structure includes the following components: ansible-automated-compliance-enforcement/ │ ├── inventory/ │ └── group_vars/ │ └── all/ │ └── vars.yml │ ├── playbooks/ │ └── compliance.yml │ ├── roles/ │ ├── compliance_checks/ │ │ ├── defaults/ │ │ │ └── main.yml │ │ └── tasks/ │ │ ├── main.yml │ │ ├── firewall.yml │ │ └── network.yml │ │ │ └── compliance_remediation/ │ └── tasks/ │ ├── main.yml │ ├── ssh.yml │ ├── firewall.yml │ └── network.yml │ ├── README.md └── .gitignore This is a partial, evidence-backed representation of the implementation. The complete repository may contain additional task files and configuration components. Why use roles? Ansible roles provide a way to organize related tasks, variables, templates and handlers. For example, instead of placing all SSH, firewall and network tasks in one file, I can organize them by responsibility. This improves: Maintainability. Reusability. Readability. Troubleshooting. Future expansion. Screenshot 6 — Project structure Capture the output of tree or find showing your actual project structure. Suggested filename: 06-project-structure.png 7. The Eight Linux Compliance Categories The framework was organized around eight security categories. Each category focuses on a different aspect of Linux server security. 7.1 SSH Security SSH is one of the most important remote administration services on a Linux server. An insecure SSH configuration can expose systems to unnecessary authentication risks. The audit examined effective SSH configuration, including: Root login restrictions. Password authentication. Public-key authentication. Maximum authentication attempts. During the initial inspection, the following values were observed: MaxAuthTries 6 PermitRootLogin without-password PubkeyAuthentication yes PasswordAuthentication no The intended stricter baseline was: PermitRootLogin no PasswordAuthentication no MaxAuthTries 4 For remediation, I prepared an Ansible-managed configuration file: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-ansible-compliance.conf An important part of safe SSH remediation is validating the configuration before reloading the daemon. The validation command is: sshd -t If validation succeeds, the configuration syntax is accepted by the SSH daemon. This helps prevent an invalid configuration from breaking remote administrative access. The project also used configuration backups and controlled service handling. The subsequent audit verified the intended effective SSH settings on both managed servers. Engineering lesson: Security hardening should not compromise the ability to administer the infrastructure. Capture the actual SSH audit output showing the effective configuration and PASS results. 7.2 Firewall Security The second category focused on UFW, the Uncomplicated Firewall. The audit inspected: Whether UFW was installed. Whether the firewall was active. Default incoming policy. SSH application profile. Commands used during the investigation included: ufw version ufw status verbose ufw app info OpenSSH One important discovery was that having UFW installed did not mean that the firewall was enabled. The initial audit identified inactive firewall status. Before enabling a firewall remotely, I verified that SSH access was permitted. The remediation sequence included allowing the OpenSSH application profile, setting default policies and enabling UFW. Subsequent audit results confirmed that UFW was active and the default incoming policy was deny. This was one of the key remediation milestones in the project. 7.3 User and Account Security User account security is important because unauthorized privileged access can compromise an entire server. The project included checks involving: Sudoers configuration validity. Sudo group membership. Admin group membership. Accounts with empty password fields. Unauthorized sudo users. One of the validation commands was: visudo -c The historical output included: /etc/sudoers: parsed OK /etc/sudoers.d/90-cloud-init-users: parsed OK The recorded audit results showed no empty-password accounts and no unauthorized sudo users under the project's defined checks. This helped establish that the inspected account configuration satisfied the implemented baseline. Capture the actual user audit results, including sudoers validation and account findings. Avoid exposing unnecessary usernames. 7.4 File and Directory Permissions Linux permissions determine who can read, write or execute files. Incorrect permissions on sensitive system files can expose information or allow unauthorized modification. The audit included important account-related files such as: File Expected permission /etc/passwd 0644 /etc/shadow 0600 The historical audit recorded both files as passing their permission checks. Understanding file ownership and permission modes is essential when automating Linux security. For example: stat -c '%a %U %G %n' /etc/passwd /etc/shadow This command displays the permissions, owner, group and filename. Capture the permission inspection output for the actual files checked by your project. 7.5 Legacy and Unnecessary Services Unnecessary services increase the attack surface of a server. The project inspected installed packages, service units and listening ports according to its configured checks. It is important to distinguish between: A package being installed. A service being enabled. A service currently running. A process listening on a network port. These are different conditions. The historical audit reported no prohibited packages, service units or listening ports under the project's configured policy. I consider this an important part of infrastructure security because unnecessary services should be reviewed rather than automatically removed without understanding their dependencies. Capture the actual service compliance output and findings. 7.6 System Updates and Patch Compliance Keeping Linux systems updated is an important security responsibility. The project inspected pending package updates and security updates. The historical findings were: Finding Per server Total pending updates 14 Security updates 11 This was a compliance finding rather than a successful patching result. I deliberately distinguish between identifying pending updates and installing them. Blindly upgrading production infrastructure can introduce compatibility problems, service interruptions or reboot requirements. A controlled patching process should consider: Maintenance windows. Package dependencies. Application compatibility. Backup and recovery. Reboot requirements. Post-update validation. The audit therefore provides useful operational visibility without automatically treating every pending update as an instruction to upgrade immediately. Capture the actual Ansible package audit output showing the number of pending updates and security updates. 7.7 Logging and Audit Configuration Logs are essential for understanding what happens on a Linux server. They support: Troubleshooting. Security investigations. Authentication monitoring. Service failure analysis. Operational accountability. The project inspected logging-related configuration, including rsyslog and systemd-journald. The historical audit recorded both facilities as passing their defined checks. The configuration also included an inspection of ForwardToSyslog . This category helps ensure that important operational logging facilities are available and configured according to the project's expectations. Capture the actual logging audit results, including the services and configuration values inspected. 7.8 Network Security Network security was one of the more interesting parts of this project. I wanted to inspect Linux kernel network parameters rather than relying only on firewall rules. The audit included: IPv4 forwarding. IPv4 ICMP redirect acceptance. IPv4 ICMP redirect sending. IPv6 forwarding. IPv6 ICMP redirect acceptance. Relevant default and interface-specific settings. I used the following command to inspect the network parameters: ansible compliance_servers -b -m shell -a \ "sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward \ net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects \ net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects \ net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects \ net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects \ net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding \ net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding \ net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects \ net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects" Discovering network interfaces Another important step was discovering the interfaces on the managed servers. I executed: ansible compliance_servers -m setup \ -a "filter=ansible_interfaces" The discovered interfaces included: lo ens5 This matters because checking only global network parameters may not reveal every interface-specific configuration. Runtime versus persistent configuration Linux sysctl parameters can be configured at runtime or persisted across reboots. For example: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward displays the current runtime value. Persistent configuration can be stored in files under: /etc/sysctl.d/ The project included a persistent security configuration file: /etc/sysctl.d/99-ansible-network-security.conf This distinction is important because a setting applied only at runtime may disappear after a reboot. The later audit verified the persistent network baseline and reported passing network checks. Capture the actual sysctl inspection output, discovered interfaces and network compliance results. 8. Separating Compliance Auditing from Remediation One of the most important architectural decisions was keeping the audit and remediation responsibilities separate. I organized the project around two roles: roles/ ├── compliance_checks/ │ └── compliance_remediation/ Audit mode Audit mode inspects the server configuration and identifies compliance findings. It should not intentionally modify the managed systems. Remediation mode Remediation mode allows the automation to apply selected security configuration changes. The intended workflow is: Gather facts | v Validate execution mode | v Run compliance audit | v Check for remediation mode | v Apply approved remediation | v Run compliance audit again | v Review final findings The project supports two execution modes: audit and: remediate The default execution mode was configured as audit. This is useful because an ordinary audit should not unexpectedly modify infrastructure. Why this design matters Imagine running a compliance check against ten production servers. You want to know which systems are misconfigured before making changes. Separating the two responsibilities allows you to inspect first, review findings and then decide whether remediation is appropriate. It also makes troubleshooting easier because you can distinguish between problems discovered during inspection and changes introduced during remediation. Screenshot 15 — Audit and remediation architecture [SCREENSHOT PLACEHOLDER 15: PLAYBOOK AND ROLE STRUCTURE] Capture the central compliance playbook and the two role directories in your project. Suggested filename: 15-audit-remediation-architecture.png 9. Safe Remediation Engineering Applying security configurations remotely requires caution. A configuration change that looks harmless can interrupt administrative access or break an application. For SSH remediation, the implementation included a configuration validation step: sshd -t For firewall remediation, SSH access was allowed before enabling UFW. For network remediation, persistent configuration was considered rather than relying only on temporary runtime changes. These are important engineering principles: Back up configurations before modifying sensitive files. Validate configuration syntax before applying service changes. Use handlers where appropriate. Avoid unnecessary service restarts. Apply changes conditionally. Re-run the audit after remediation. Consider rollback and recovery procedures. A particularly important Ansible concept here is idempotency. Idempotency means that if I execute the same automation again, Ansible should recognize that the desired configuration is already present and avoid unnecessary changes. This is important for repeatable infrastructure management. I also learned that changed=0 does not necessarily mean every security requirement has passed. A server can remain unchanged while the audit identifies outstanding compliance gaps. 10. Troubleshooting and Engineering Lessons Building this project involved more than writing task files. Several issues required investigation. Challenge 1: Incorrect SSH private-key path Problem: Ansible could not connect to the managed servers because the configured private-key path was incorrect. Investigation: I compared the inventory configuration with the actual key location and tested SSH connectivity. Resolution: I corrected the key path and restricted its file permissions. Lesson: Always verify the actual SSH key path and test manual SSH before troubleshooting Ansible itself. Challenge 2: Firewall installed but inactive Problem: The initial audit showed that UFW was installed but inactive. Investigation: I checked firewall status and verified the OpenSSH application profile. Resolution: I implemented remediation that allowed SSH before enabling the firewall. Lesson: Remote firewall changes must be designed around administrator access and recovery. Challenge 3: Effective SSH configuration Problem: The effective SSH configuration did not initially match the intended security baseline. Investigation: I inspected effective SSH settings rather than assuming that the main configuration file represented the active configuration. Resolution: I prepared an Ansible-managed SSH configuration and validated the effective values after remediation. Lesson: Configuration files and effective runtime configuration are not always the same. Challenge 4: Network interface discovery Problem: Global network settings alone were not sufficient for a complete network security assessment. Investigation: I gathered Ansible facts to identify available network interfaces. Resolution: I incorporated interface-aware inspection and persistent sysctl checks. Lesson: Security auditing needs to consider the actual configuration of the system, including individual interfaces. Challenge 5: Outstanding package updates Problem: The audit identified pending security updates. Investigation: I inspected package update information and distinguished security updates from other updates. Resolution: The framework reported outstanding patches rather than automatically installing everything. Lesson: Compliance automation should support operational decisions, not blindly make potentially disruptive changes. 11. Executing and Validating the Framework I used several Ansible commands throughout the implementation. Inspect inventory ansible-inventory --graph This displays the inventory hierarchy and managed host groups. Test connectivity ansible compliance_servers -m ping This confirms Ansible connectivity and remote module execution. Validate playbook syntax ansible-playbook playbooks/compliance.yml --syntax-check This checks the playbook for syntax and structural issues. Execute the compliance audit ansible-playbook playbooks/compliance.yml Explicitly select audit mode ansible-playbook playbooks/compliance.yml \ -e compliance_mode = audit Execute remediation mode ansible-playbook playbooks/compliance.yml \ -e compliance_mode = remediate Remediation should only be executed against systems where you have reviewed the intended changes and have an appropriate recovery plan. Historical audit execution A later recorded audit execution produced the following results on both managed servers: Ansible result Per server OK 52 Changed 0 Failed 0 Skipped 70 Unreachable 0 An earlier execution reported a different recap, including 65 skipped tasks. These were separate runs and should not be combined. Understanding the results ok : A task completed without requiring a change. changed : A task modified the system. failed : A task encountered an error. skipped : A task was not executed because of a condition or other execution rule. unreachable : Ansible could not establish the required connection to the host. The absence of failed tasks means the automation completed without reported task failures. It does not automatically mean that every compliance check passed. That is why I also examined the actual compliance findings. Screenshot 16 — Playbook execution Capture the actual final audit execution showing both hosts, their task summaries and the recap. 12. What the Project Revealed The historical audit results showed that seven of the eight categories passed their defined checks, while the system update category continued to identify pending packages. Category Recorded result SSH security PASS Firewall security PASS User security PASS File permissions PASS Legacy services PASS System updates FINDINGS Logging PASS Network security PASS These results represent the project's recorded audit findings, not an independent security certification. The update findings remained important: 14 total pending updates per server. 11 security updates per server. The framework successfully identified these outstanding items instead of hiding them behind a successful Ansible execution summary. For me, this was one of the most important outcomes of the project. A useful compliance automation system must identify problems accurately, not simply report that its playbook executed successfully. 13. Reporting and Future Improvements Structured compliance reporting is an important direction for this project. A JSON report could make the audit findings easier to consume in external systems. For example, a future report could contain: Hostname. Audit timestamp. Compliance category. Individual check. Expected configuration. Actual configuration. Pass or fail status. Remediation status. A simplified example of the intended reporting structure might look like this: { "hostname" : "compliance-server-01" , "compliance" : { "ssh" : { "status" : "PASS" } , "firewall" : { "status" : "PASS" } , "system_updates" : { "status" : "FAIL" , "pending_updates" : 14 , "security_updates" : 11 } } } This is an illustrative future report format, not a claim that this exact JSON file was generated by the current implementation. Other improvements I would like to introduce include: Ansible Vault for managing sensitive variables. Ansible-lint and YAML linting. Molecule testing for reusable roles. CI/CD validation through GitHub Actions. Historical compliance reports. Centralized reporting and dashboards. Scheduled compliance audits. More comprehensive rollback and recovery procedures. Integration with AWS Systems Manager and other security tooling. These improvements would help evolve the project into a more comprehensive infrastructure compliance automation solution. 14. Key Lessons Learned This project reinforced several important engineering principles. 1. Automation starts with understanding the infrastructure. Before writing automation, I needed to understand SSH connectivity, Linux configuration, firewall behaviour and network interfaces. 2. Ansible roles improve maintainability. Separating audit and remediation made the project easier to understand and extend. 3. Security remediation must be controlled. A security improvement should not accidentally lock administrators out of their own servers. 4. Effective configuration matters. Inspecting the effective SSH configuration was more useful than simply reading a configuration file. 5. Runtime and persistent settings are different. This became especially important during network security auditing. 6. A successful playbook is not the same as a compliant server. The actual security findings matter more than the execution recap alone. 7. Verification is part of automation. Applying a configuration change is only one part of the process. Re-running the audit establishes whether the intended result was achieved. 15. Conclusion Building this Ansible Automated Compliance Enforcement framework gave me practical experience in applying infrastructure automation to Linux security. I worked through SSH connectivity problems, configured an Ansible inventory, organized reusable roles, inspected eight security categories and implemented controlled remediation for important security configurations. More importantly, I learned to distinguish between auditing, identifying compliance gaps, applying changes and verifying the resulting configuration. The project is still open to improvement, particularly around structured reporting, automated testing and broader integration with cloud security tooling. However, it has provided a practical foundation for understanding how Ansible can help standardize Linux security checks across multiple cloud servers. My next goal is to continue improving the framework, strengthen its reporting capabilities and make it easier for other engineers to reproduce. The main lesson: infrastructure automation should not just execute commands. It should provide consistency, visibility, controlled changes and verifiable results. Thank you for reading!

title: Turn Free Web AIs (DeepSeek, Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude) into a Local MCP Agent Harness
author: Astrax
summary: A raw LLM in a browser tab is just a text predictor—what turns models like DeepSeek, Gemini, ChatGPT, or Claude into real autonomous agents is the agent harness around them. I built Web MCP Bridge to wrap their free web interfaces in a complete local Model Context Protocol (MCP) harness using a Manifest V3 extension and a lightweight Python WebSocket bridge ( 127.0.0.1 ). By plugging in local stdio MCP servers—including REA for reverse engineering, Craft Anything for 3D modeling, FFmpeg/Remotion for video editing, or full filesystem and terminal access—you can code, edit videos, model 3D assets, and automate complex workflows with zero API keys, zero subscriptions, and zero local GPUs required. In v1.8.0 , the bridge scales to hundreds of tools without freezing browser tabs by replacing massive 100k-character schema dumps with a compact ~2k-character paginated catalog ( list_tools ) that models query on demand. It also introduces a 3-layer self-healing JSON parser to fix broken model outputs (such as unescaped Windows paths or trailing commas), a redesigned bilingual UI (EN/ES), and dual licensing under MIT and Apache 2.0 . Everything runs 100% locally on your machine: the bridge rejects non-extension origins, isolates tool outputs to prevent prompt injection, and defaults to "Ask every time" so nothing runs without your explicit approval. Grab the code and quick-start guide on GitHub: AstraxOf/web-mcp-bridge

title: How to Remove Blank Pages from PDF with Python
author: Jack9012
summary: Unwanted blank pages can appear when scanning, merging, or exporting PDFs. For example, duplex scanning may capture the empty backs of sheets, while document layouts can generate unnecessary blank pages. Finding and deleting these pages manually can be time-consuming. With Python, you can automate page detection and cleanup. However, a page that looks blank does not necessarily contain no content. It may include a solid white image or invisible text. This article combines Spire.PDF for Python with Pillow to check whether PDF pages are blank, perform an additional check on rendered page images, and remove pages that meet the criteria. 1. Install the Dependencies and Prepare a File This example uses two libraries: Spire.PDF for Python : Loads PDFs, detects blank pages, renders pages, and removes and saves pages. Pillow : Reads the rendered page images and examines their pixels. Run the following command in your terminal: pip install Spire.PDF Pillow Prepare a file named Sample.pdf and place it in your Python script's working directory. To observe the results, you can include regular content pages, blank pages, and pages containing only a solid white image in the test file. 2. How Blank Page Detection Works This example uses two levels of detection: Call the page's IsBlank() method. If it returns True , remove the page directly. For pages not identified as blank, use SaveAsImage() to render each page as an image. Then use Pillow to check whether every pixel is pure white. If so, remove that page as well. This combined approach is also used in Spire.PDF's official blank page removal example. It can help identify some pages that contain page objects but appear entirely white when rendered. One distinction is essential: the image check requires every pixel to be pure white; it does not detect pages that are merely “almost blank.” If the rendered image contains even one pixel that is not pure white, the image check will not classify the page as blank. Pages with gray backgrounds, scanning noise, or page numbers will therefore generally be retained. 3. Complete Code: Detect and Remove Blank Pages The following code keeps both levels of detection and places the input and output paths together so you can easily change the files. import io from spire . pdf import PdfDocument from PIL import Image # Check whether every pixel in the image is pure white def is_blank_image ( image ) : with image . convert ( "RGB" ) as rgb_image : white_pixel = ( 255 , 255 , 255 ) return all ( pixel == white_pixel for pixel in rgb_image . getdata ( ) ) # 1. Set the input and output files input_path = "Sample.pdf" output_path = "RemoveBlankPages.pdf" # 2. Load the PDF document pdf = PdfDocument ( ) pdf . LoadFromFile ( input_path ) original_page_count = pdf . Pages . Count removed_page_numbers = [ ] # 3. Detect and remove blank pages, starting from the last page for i in range ( original_page_count - 1 , - 1 , - 1 ) : page = pdf . Pages . get_Item ( i ) # First, use the PDF page's blank detection method if page . IsBlank ( ) : pdf . Pages . RemoveAt ( i ) removed_page_numbers . append ( i + 1 ) continue # For the remaining pages, render an image and check its pixels with pdf . SaveAsImage ( i ) as image_data : image_bytes = image_data . ToArray ( ) with io . BytesIO ( image_bytes ) as image_stream : with Image . open ( image_stream ) as image : if is_blank_image ( image ) : pdf . Pages . RemoveAt ( i ) removed_page_numbers . append ( i + 1 ) # 4. Save the result and close the document remaining_page_count = pdf . Pages . Count if remaining_page_count > 0 : pdf . SaveToFile ( output_path ) pdf . Close ( ) # 5. Print processing information removed_page_numbers . sort ( ) print ( f "Original page count: {original_page_count}" ) print ( f "Pages removed: {len(removed_page_numbers)}" ) print ( f "Original page numbers removed: {removed_page_numbers}" ) if remaining_page_count > 0 : print ( f "Result saved to: {output_path}" ) else : print ( "No pages remain. The output file was not saved." ) If every page is removed, the code skips saving to avoid attempting to create a PDF with no pages. Using different filenames for the input and output also preserves the original document for comparison. 4. Understanding the Key Parts of the Code 4.1. Check for Pure White Using RGB Pixels The is_blank_image() function first converts the image to RGB mode, then checks whether each pixel equals (255, 255, 255) . all() returns True only when every pixel meets this condition. It stops checking as soon as it encounters a non-white pixel. As a result, a pure white page requires checking every pixel, while a page containing visible content may finish the check earlier. 4.2. Why Remove Pages in Reverse Order? PDF page indices start at 0 . When a page is removed, the indices of subsequent pages shift down. If you iterate from the first page and delete pages as you go, you may skip the page immediately following a deleted page. The code processes pages backward, starting from the last page: for i in range ( original_page_count - 1 , - 1 , - 1 ) : This ensures that removing the current page does not change the indices of earlier pages that have yet to be processed. It also makes it straightforward to record each removed page's original page number. 4.3. Does Rendering Affect the Pages That Are Retained? The images in this example are used only for detection and are not written back into the PDF. The program removes blank pages directly from the original document's page collection and saves the remaining pages. It does not rebuild the entire document as an image-based PDF. 5. Scope and Considerations Pure white detection works best for clean blank pages. Scanned “blank” pages often still contain gray backgrounds, paper texture, or dark specks, all of which cause the pixel check to return False . To handle these scans, you can introduce a near-white color threshold and a limit on the proportion of non-white pixels. However, these settings need to be tested with real samples to avoid misclassifying faint text or thin lines as blank. A visually blank page may still contain useful data. Some pages may include hidden text, links, or interactive elements. Even if the rendered result is white, the page may still be worth retaining. When using visual detection, decide whether to remove such pages based on the document's intended use. Rendering adds processing time. Pages for which IsBlank() returns True are removed directly; only the remaining pages undergo image detection. For PDFs with many pages or large page dimensions, rendering and pixel-by-pixel checking may take considerable time. After running the script, check the output page count and the list of removed pages, paying particular attention to pages with faint content. If your environment has evaluation restrictions or evaluation watermarks, also verify whether they affect page rendering and detection results. 6. Conclusion With Spire.PDF for Python and Pillow, you can remove blank PDF pages by combining page-level blank detection with a pure white check on rendered page images. Reverse iteration avoids index changes during deletion, while the strict pure white criterion clearly defines the scope of detection. Scanned blank pages containing noise require additional tolerance rules and testing to check for unintended deletions.

title: TradingView UT Bot Strategy: Heikin Ashi Backtest Is Fake
author: Truong Pham | Moon The Train
summary: The short version. This TradingView UT Bot strategy backtest starts with the Heikin Ashi trap: on an HA chart the strategy looks like a money machine, and at real prices it isn't. It also covers the settings and repainting. The script is UT Bot Strategy by QuantNomad, one of the most-boosted open-source strategies on TradingView. I ported it line for line to Python and ran it on Exness tick data with real spread and commission: five forex and gold markets from 2020 to 2026, Bitcoin from 2024, and gold back to 2004. The Heikin Ashi chart backtest is fake. Put the strategy on a Heikin Ashi chart and it shows PF 8.6 to 11.5 with 65–69% winners on every market and timeframe I tried (gold, EURUSD, Bitcoin, M5 to H4). Fill the same signals at real prices and it's PF 0.90 to 1.19 with 35–38% winners. The table and the equity chart below show both side by side. Forex lost money on every timeframe. EURUSD, GBPUSD, NZDUSD and USDJPY: profit factor 0.52 to 1.00 from M5 to D1 after costs. Gold H4 is the only real positive. PF 1.17 on 1,219 trades, +2,245 USD per 0.01 lot. But 2020 to 2022 lost money, and the ten best trades made more than the whole result. Gold 2004–2019, data I didn't use to pick H4: PF 1.00. Sixteen years of break-even. M5 and M15 lose everywhere. About 35–40 trades a day, and the spread eats all of it. My verdict: UT Bot is a plain ATR trailing stop that flips long and short. It doesn't have an edge on its own. If you've seen a UT Bot backtest with a 70–90% win rate, check the chart type first. What is the UT Bot strategy on TradingView? It's a trailing stop that sits one ATR away from price and flips the trade when a candle closes on the other side of it. The UT Bot Strategy page is QuantNomad's strategy version of the "UT Bot" indicator by Yo_adriiiiaan, which credits HPotter for the idea. It's dated 15 November 2019, Pine v4, and had 9,114 boosts when I checked in November 2026. The "UT Bot Strategy with Backtesting Range" by the same author has identical rules plus a date filter, so this review covers both. Three inputs: Key Value (default 1), ATR Period (default 10) and a checkbox Signals from Heikin Ashi Candles (off). Here's the core of the Pine code: xATR = atr(c) nLoss = a * xATR xATRTrailingStop := iff(src > nz(xATRTrailingStop[1], 0) and src[1] > nz(xATRTrailingStop[1], 0), max(nz(xATRTrailingStop[1]), src - nLoss), iff(src < nz(xATRTrailingStop[1], 0) and src[1] < nz(xATRTrailingStop[1], 0), min(nz(xATRTrailingStop[1]), src + nLoss), iff(src > nz(xATRTrailingStop[1], 0), src - nLoss, src + nLoss))) ... buy = src > xATRTrailingStop and crossover(ema(src, 1), xATRTrailingStop) sell = src < xATRTrailingStop and crossover(xATRTrailingStop, ema(src, 1)) strategy.entry("long", true, when = buy) strategy.entry("short", false, when = sell) In plain words: while price stays above the line, the line moves up to close − Key × ATR and never moves down. When a close drops below it, the line jumps above price and starts following it down. Each crossing is a buy or a sell. ema(src, 1) is just the close itself. There's no stop loss or take profit. The line is the stop, but it's only checked at the candle close, and the strategy is always in the market, long or short. Here's what that looks like on gold H4 with the defaults: Gold went from about 3,350 to 4,350 in those eight weeks. UT Bot still flipped short 15 times, because a stop one ATR away gets hit by any normal pullback. The longs made +557 USD per 0.01 lot, the shorts lost 387, so it kept +171 of a 1,000-dollar move. In a range it's worse: Twelve trades in three weeks, net −234. That's the whole pattern of this strategy in two pictures. Should you use UT Bot on Heikin Ashi candles? Use the checkbox if you like, but don't put the strategy on a Heikin Ashi chart. The author says the same thing on the script page: "Do not add this strategy to HA candles, use usual candles and this checkbox." This is where most of the amazing UT Bot backtests on YouTube come from, so it's worth showing why. Heikin Ashi candles aren't real prices. The HA open is the average of the previous HA open and close, so it lags the market. When the strategy runs on an HA chart, TradingView fills the orders at those HA prices unless you change the fill setting in the strategy properties. So the backtest buys at a price that's usually below where the market actually was, and sells above it. I ran the same signals both ways, no costs, as TradingView shows by default: No costs Strategy on an HA chart Same signals at real prices XAUUSD H1 PF 11.26, 67% winners PF 1.12, 36% winners XAUUSD H4 PF 10.81, 68% PF 1.19, 38% EURUSD M15 PF 9.99, 67% PF 0.94, 36% EURUSD H4 PF 11.52, 69% PF 1.05, 38% BTCUSD M5 PF 9.39, 66% PF 1.04, 36% BTCUSD H1 PF 10.15, 66% PF 1.01, 36% Exness ticks, gold and EURUSD Jan 2020 – Sep 2026, BTCUSD Jan 2024 – Nov 2026, Key 1 and ATR 10. It doesn't matter what market or timeframe you pick. The HA chart turns a coin flip into a money printer, and none of that money exists: And the checkbox, which reads the HA close but trades at real prices, doesn't rescue anything either. After costs: gold H1 1.10, gold H4 1.18, EURUSD M5 to H1 0.70 to 0.85, BTCUSD M5 to H4 0.90 to 0.98. Does UT Bot repaint? No, not on normal candles. The strategy decides at the bar close and fills at the next bar's open. The Heikin Ashi option uses security() on the same timeframe with lookahead = false , so it doesn't look ahead on historical bars either. The line on the live, unfinished candle can move while the candle is open, which is why the signal sometimes appears and disappears in real time. The strategy only acts once the bar closes. The thing that misleads people isn't repainting. It's the HA chart fills above. What does the author claim? Nothing about performance. QuantNomad says they took Yo_adriiiiaan's code, cleaned it up, moved it to Pine v4, made a strategy from it and added the Heikin Ashi checkbox. There are no profit claims, no suggested market and no suggested timeframe. So I tested the defaults across everything I had. How I tested it Port: Python, line for line, including Pine's nz(stop[1], 0) start-up and the RMA-based atr() . Signals at the bar close, fills at the next bar's open, stop-and-reverse like strategy.entry . Data: Exness Raw Spread tick archives for XAUUSD, EURUSD, GBPUSD, USDJPY and NZDUSD, January 2020 to September 2026. BTCUSD from January 2024 to November 2026, which is all the tick history I have for it. Costs: buys fill at the real ask on the first tick of the bar, sells at the bid, plus 3.5 USD per lot per side on forex and gold, 1 USD per BTC per side on Bitcoin. Swap gets its own line further down. Older gold data: Dukascopy M1 bars via Tickstory, 2004 to July 2026, spread from the data, swap on longs scaled to the gold price of the time. Size: fixed, no compounding. Gold in USD per 0.01 lot (one ounce), forex in pips, Bitcoin in USD per 1 BTC. Is the TradingView backtest accurate? The signals, yes. The money, no, and less so the lower the timeframe. The script sets no commission and TradingView's tester can't model spread or swap (I went through this in the SuperTrend backtest ). UT Bot trades a lot, so this matters more than usual: Default settings, long + short Trades PF, no costs PF, real costs Net, no costs → real Gold M5 61,372 1.00 0.90 +286 → −9,527 USD Gold H4 1,219 1.19 1.17 +2,437 → +2,245 USD EURUSD M5 68,889 0.90 0.66 −17,660 → −76,718 pips USDJPY M15 20,362 1.00 0.83 +587 → −26,370 pips BTCUSD M5 36,295 1.02 0.90 +78,215 → −384,201 USD On a TradingView-style test, gold M5 and BTC M5 look like small winners. With the spread they're the worst results in the whole study. The results Profit factor after spread and commission, default Key 1 / ATR 10: Red everywhere below H1. Forex stays red on every timeframe. The blue cells are gold H4/D1 and Bitcoin D1, and the Bitcoin D1 cell has 109 trades in under three years, which is too few to trust. Gold (XAUUSD Raw Spread), 29 Jan 2020 – Sep 2026, before swap: Timeframe Direction Trades Win rate PF Net Max drawdown M5 long + short 61,372 33.1% 0.90 −9,527 11,026 M15 long + short 19,483 34.2% 0.93 −4,100 4,383 H1 long + short 4,565 35.7% 1.04 +931 1,099 H4 long + short 1,219 37.2% 1.17 +2,245 809 H4 long only 609 39.2% 1.38 +2,413 816 D1 long + short 239 42.3% 1.07 +459 1,807 Buy and hold 1 +2,591 1,579 Net and drawdown in USD per 0.01 lot, drawdown on open equity. "Long only" isn't a script setting; I added it to see where the money came from. The shorts lost money on gold on every timeframe. On H4 they cost 168, so the long-only version did slightly better than the default, and neither beat buying gold and holding it. Is the gold H4 result real? Probably not, or at least not in a way you could count on. Four things point the same way: It all came from two years. Gold H4 by exit year: 2020 PF 0.96, 2021 0.97, 2022 0.84, 2023 1.20, 2024 0.98, 2025 1.35, 2026 1.38. The 2025–2026 profit (+2,380) is bigger than the six-and-a-half-year total. A handful of trades carry it. The ten best trades made +2,460. The other 1,209 trades lost 216 together. Random timing comes close. I slid the strategy's own long/short pattern to a random point in time, 300 times. Same trades, same holding times, no link to price. The real result (+2,245) beat most copies (median −3), but 6.6% of the random copies did as well or better. Gold H1 was weaker: 19% of random copies beat it. Before 2020 it broke even. Below. Does it work on gold before 2020? No. I ran the default settings on Dukascopy gold from 2004 to 2019, a period I hadn't looked at when choosing H4. The spread in that data is wider than an Exness Raw account, so the low timeframes get hit even harder, but H4 and D1 shouldn't care much. Gold, 2004–2019 Trades PF after swap Summed return M5 long + short 134,789 0.61 −4,421% M15 long + short 42,685 0.74 −1,523% H1 long + short 10,297 0.89 −333% H4 long + short 2,694 1.00 −11.5% H4 long only 1,347 1.05 +50% D1 long only 284 1.16 +67% Fixed size, no compounding. "Summed return" adds each trade's profit as a percent of its entry price. Gold itself rose 266% over the period. The long-only line made a little while gold was rising (2004–2011) and gave some back after. The default long + short line went nowhere for sixteen years and was still negative in 2024. Only the 2025 rally pulled it up. What are the best UT Bot settings? There aren't any that hold up. I ran Key 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 against ATR 1, 3, 5, 10, 14, 20 and 50, with and without the Heikin Ashi checkbox. That's 84 combinations per market and timeframe, long + short, all after costs: Market Combos with PF > 1 Profitable in both halves Median PF XAUUSD M15 (long + short) 37 / 84 6 0.98 XAUUSD H1 76 / 84 39 1.08 XAUUSD H4 84 / 84 48 1.18 EURUSD M15 0 / 84 0 0.84 EURUSD H1 5 / 84 3 0.87 USDJPY H1 57 / 84 42 1.03 NZDUSD H1 and H4 0 / 84 0 0.87 BTCUSD H1 9 / 84 6 0.95 "Both halves" = profitable in the first and in the second half of the data. Halves for gold are Jan 2020 – May 2023 and May 2023 – Sep 2026. Gold H4 looks great until you split it. Here are the 42 settings without Heikin Ashi, each half on its own: A bigger Key (3 or 4) means a looser stop, so the strategy stays in the trend longer. That's exactly what paid in the 2024–2026 rally (PF mostly 1.7 to 2.4). In 2020 to mid-2023, when gold chopped around, the same settings made 0.73 to 1.24. Key 4 with ATR 14 went from 0.73 to 2.06. If you optimize UT Bot on recent gold data you'll pick a big Key, and you'll be picking the last rally. On 2004–2019 gold the grid says the same: median PF 1.02 on H4 and 0.97 on H1, and only a few settings made money in both 2004–2011 and 2012–2019. How does it compare with Hull Suite, PMax and SuperTrend? It's the weakest of the four on gold. Same Exness data, same costs, default settings, long + short: Gold, Jan 2020 – Sep 2026 H1 PF H4 PF UT Bot 1.04 1.17 Hull Suite 1.28 1.25 PMax 1.37 0.98 SuperTrend 1.09 1.90 All four are trend followers. The difference is mostly how far the stop sits from price, and UT Bot's default of one ATR is the tightest. Risk structure No stop loss beyond the line, and the line only counts at the close. The worst gold H4 trade was a buy at 4,725.86 on 20 March 2026, closed at 4,553.56 twelve hours later: −172 USD per 0.01 lot, after being 249 underwater. Whipsaws come in pairs. On 29 January 2026 a short at 5,182.88 lost 123, and the buy that replaced it lost 109 by the next morning. Nine of the ten worst gold H4 trades were in 2026 , with gold at 4,000 to 5,300. A fixed lot risks more as price rises. Swap. Gold H4 trades last 48 hours on average (longest 284). Swap on longs, scaled to price, takes gold H4 from +2,245 to +1,815 (PF 1.14). Losing streaks. The longest run of losers on gold H4 was 10 trades. The win rate is 37%. That's normal for trend following, but you need the big winners to show up, and in 2020–2022 they mostly didn't. What isn't a red flag: no martingale, no grid, no averaging. Who should use it? Honestly, I wouldn't trade it as a strategy. As a visual trailing stop for trades you take for other reasons, a bigger Key (2 to 4) on H4 or higher is reasonable, and it's simple to read. As an automated system with the defaults, it lost on forex, lost below H1 everywhere, and only made money on gold H4 because of the 2025–2026 rally. If you want a trend filter for gold, Hull Suite held up better on the same data. What I couldn't verify TradingView itself. My HA-chart numbers come from my port, filling at HA open prices the way TradingView's default does. I didn't export TradingView's own report. Forex swap. Not included in the forex numbers. It wouldn't turn PF 0.66 into a winner. Bitcoin before 2024. I only have Exness BTC ticks from January 2024, so the BTC results cover under three years. Other brokers, stocks and indices. Exness data only, forex, gold and Bitcoin only. Daily candles. Mine close at UTC midnight; TradingView forex daily bars usually close at 17:00 New York. Bottom line The TradingView UT Bot strategy doesn't repaint and doesn't make money with its default settings: forex lost on every timeframe, M5 and M15 lost everywhere, and gold H4 (PF 1.17) came from one rally and broke even from 2004 to 2019. The 70–90% win-rate backtests come from running it on a Heikin Ashi chart, where it fills at prices that never traded. This is part of a series where I take the most-boosted open-source TradingView strategies, port them exactly and test them on broker ticks with real costs. The Hull Suite backtest uses the same data if you want to compare. I'm not affiliated with TradingView, QuantNomad, Yo_adriiiiaan or HPotter. Past results, including backtests, don't guarantee future results.

title: Plataforma MLOps para modelos bayesianos: del notebook a producción con autonomía y control
author: Julián Cardozo
summary: Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io . Un modelo bayesiano bien construido no responde solo «cuánto», sino también «con qué incertidumbre». Esa propiedad, que es su principal valor para el negocio, es también lo que lo vuelve más difícil de operar: el entrenamiento depende de un muestreo que puede no converger, el artefacto es una distribución y no un vector de pesos, y una predicción puntual correcta puede esconder intervalos mal calibrados. Este artículo recorre el trabajo de un equipo de plataforma que da soporte a Data Scientists que construyen este tipo de modelos: templates, validación automática, promoción entre entornos con MLflow, herramientas de despliegue y reversión, serving, monitoreo, gobernanza y formación. El objetivo es concreto: que la mayoría de los despliegues ocurran sin intervención del equipo de plataforma y sin perder control. El problema: autonomía sin perder control En muchas organizaciones, llevar un modelo a producción sigue siendo un proyecto en sí mismo. El Data Scientist termina un notebook, abre un ticket y espera a que alguien de ingeniería empaquete el modelo, escriba una API, configure el despliegue y agregue algo de monitoreo. Cada paso se negocia de nuevo, el conocimiento queda en pocas personas y los modelos llegan tarde o no llegan. La respuesta habitual es una plataforma de ML: un conjunto de herramientas, templates y procesos que permiten a los Data Scientists desplegar por su cuenta. Un objetivo frecuente es que al menos el 80% de los despliegues se completen sin intervención del equipo de plataforma. La cifra sirve como meta solo si se define cómo se mide: por ejemplo, la proporción de promociones a producción que no requirieron un ticket ni una sesión de soporte en los últimos 90 días. Sin esa definición, la autonomía se vuelve una percepción. Autonomía no significa ausencia de controles. Significa que los controles están automatizados, son visibles y se ejecutan siempre igual, de modo que un Data Scientist puede saber de antemano qué tiene que cumplir su modelo para llegar a producción y por qué fue rechazado si no lo cumple. Qué cambia con un modelo bayesiano La mayor parte de las prácticas de MLOps se pensaron para modelos que se entrenan con optimización y producen un conjunto de parámetros. Un modelo bayesiano ajustado con MCMC (Markov Chain Monte Carlo) produce otra cosa: muestras de la distribución posterior de sus parámetros. Esa diferencia afecta a cada etapa del ciclo. Diferencias operativas entre un modelo entrenado por optimización y uno bayesiano ajustado con MCMC Etapa Modelo por optimización Modelo bayesiano con MCMC Consecuencia para la plataforma Entrenamiento Converge a un óptimo; la pérdida indica progreso Las cadenas pueden no converger aunque el proceso termine sin error Los diagnósticos de convergencia son un gate obligatorio Artefacto Pesos del modelo Miles de muestras de la posterior, a veces de cientos de MB Hay que decidir qué se guarda para diagnóstico y qué se sirve Predicción Una pasada por el modelo Una predicción por muestra, luego se resume La latencia depende de cuántas muestras se usan Calidad Error de la predicción puntual Error y calibración de los intervalos Las métricas de monitoreo incluyen cobertura Costo Entrenamiento relativamente predecible Depende de la geometría de la posterior Conviene medir muestras efectivas por segundo Hay un punto que suele sorprender a equipos que vienen de otros tipos de modelos: un muestreo que termina sin error puede producir resultados inválidos . Cadenas que no se mezclaron, transiciones divergentes o pocas muestras efectivas generan una posterior que no representa al modelo. Por eso los diagnósticos no son una buena práctica opcional, sino una condición para registrar una versión. Una arquitectura de referencia La arquitectura que sigue es una propuesta propia. Separa cuatro responsabilidades: el código del modelo, que pertenece al Data Scientist; la validación, que la plataforma define y ejecuta; el registro y la promoción, que usan MLflow como fuente de verdad; y el serving y el monitoreo, que la plataforma opera. Ciclo de vida de un modelo en la plataforma: el diagrama se puede ver en el artículo original . Dos decisiones importan más que el resto. La primera es que el registro es la única fuente de verdad sobre qué versión corre en cada entorno : el servicio no conoce números de versión, solo aliases. La segunda es que promover y revertir son operaciones sobre el registro, no despliegues de infraestructura : mover un alias es rápido, auditable y reversible, y el servicio toma la nueva versión al recargar el modelo. Templates: el camino más corto debe ser el correcto Un template de repositorio es la forma más eficaz de difundir buenas prácticas, porque las incorpora antes de que alguien tenga que recordarlas. Conviene mantener al menos dos: uno para el modelo y otro para la API que lo sirve cuando el caso necesita lógica propia. Herramientas como Copier o Cookiecutter generan el repositorio; Copier además permite actualizar proyectos existentes cuando el template evoluciona, algo valioso cuando hay decenas de modelos. Contenido mínimo de los templates (propuesta) Template Incluye Por qué Modelo Estructura src/ con modelo.py , entrenar.py y serving.py ; datos simulados para pruebas; suite de validación de la plataforma; pipeline de CI; MODEL_CARD.md El Data Scientist escribe el modelo; todo lo demás ya está resuelto Modelo Configuración de muestreo con semilla, cadenas y umbrales declarados en un archivo Los gates son explícitos y revisables en el código API FastAPI con contrato de entrada y salida, health checks, carga por alias, métricas y trazas Cada servicio expone las mismas señales al monitoreo Ambos Dependencias fijadas, pre-commit , documentación con MkDocs Reproducibilidad y documentación desde el primer commit El template no debería esconder el modelo detrás de abstracciones propias. Un Data Scientist que usa PyMC tiene que poder escribir PyMC. La plataforma aporta la estructura alrededor, no un lenguaje nuevo. Un ejemplo verificado: de PyMC a producción con MLflow El ejemplo implementa un modelo jerárquico de demanda por tienda, la suite de validación, el registro en MLflow y las herramientas ml-deploy y ml-rollback . Usa PyMC 6.4, ArviZ 1.3, MLflow 3.18 y Typer, con Python 3.12. Qué se verificó: El código se ejecutó con esas versiones contra un registro de MLflow local sobre SQLite. Cuatro pruebas automáticas pasan: recuperación de parámetros con datos simulados, promoción y reversión con la CLI, rechazo de una versión no validada y carga del modelo por alias para predecir. Los tiempos que se mencionan corresponden a una laptop y sirven solo como orden de magnitud. El modelo modelo.py: modelo jerárquico con parametrización no centrada import pymc as pm def construir ( tienda , precio , y , n_tiendas ) : with pm . Model ( ) as m : mu_a = pm . Normal ( "mu_a" , 40 , 20 ) sigma_a = pm . HalfNormal ( "sigma_a" , 10 ) z = pm . Normal ( "z" , 0 , 1 , shape = n_tiendas ) # no centrada a = pm . Deterministic ( "a" , mu_a + z * sigma_a ) beta = pm . Normal ( "beta" , 0 , 5 ) sigma = pm . HalfNormal ( "sigma" , 10 ) pm . Normal ( "y" , a [ tienda ] + beta * precio , sigma , observed = y ) return m def ajustar ( datos , draws = 1000 , tune = 1000 , chains = 4 , seed = 42 , target_accept = 0.95 ) : m = construir ( datos [ "tienda" ] , datos [ "precio" ] , datos [ "y" ] , datos [ "n_tiendas" ] ) with m : return pm . sample ( draws = draws , tune = tune , chains = chains , random_seed = seed , target_accept = target_accept , progressbar = False , quiet = True ) Cada tienda tiene su propio nivel de demanda, pero los niveles comparten una distribución común. Así, una tienda con pocos datos toma información de las demás. La parametrización no centrada ( a = mu_a + z * sigma_a ) es una práctica estándar en modelos jerárquicos: evita una geometría de la posterior que dificulta el muestreo y suele reducir las divergencias. Los gates de validación validacion.py: convergencia, calibración y latencia como condiciones explícitas import arviz as az UMBRALES = { "rhat_max" : 1.01 , "ess_bulk_min" : 400 , "divergencias_max" : 0 , "cobertura_90_min" : 0.85 , "cobertura_90_max" : 0.95 , "latencia_p95_ms_max" : 50 } def convergencia ( idata , var_names = ( "mu_a" , "sigma_a" , "beta" , "sigma" , "a" ) ) : rhat = az . rhat ( idata , var_names = list ( var_names ) ) ess = az . ess ( idata , var_names = list ( var_names ) , method = "bulk" ) return { "rhat_max" : float ( max ( rhat [ v ] . max ( ) for v in var_names ) ) , "ess_bulk_min" : float ( min ( ess [ v ] . min ( ) for v in var_names ) ) , "divergencias" : int ( idata . sample_stats [ "diverging" ] . sum ( ) ) , } def evaluar ( metricas , u = UMBRALES ) : fallas = [ ] if metricas [ "rhat_max" ] > u [ "rhat_max" ] : fallas . append ( "rhat" ) if metricas [ "ess_bulk_min" ] < u [ "ess_bulk_min" ] : fallas . append ( "ess" ) if metricas [ "divergencias" ] > u [ "divergencias_max" ] : fallas . append ( "divergencias" ) if not u [ "cobertura_90_min" ] <= metricas [ "cobertura_90" ] <= u [ "cobertura_90_max" ] : fallas . append ( "cobertura" ) if metricas [ "latencia_p95_ms" ] > u [ "latencia_p95_ms_max" ] : fallas . append ( "latencia" ) return fallas Los umbrales de R-hat (1,01) y de tamaño efectivo de muestra (400 en total entre cadenas) siguen las recomendaciones de Vehtari y colegas en su revisión del diagnóstico R-hat. La cobertura mide qué proporción de observaciones nuevas cae dentro del intervalo del 90%: si el modelo está bien calibrado, debería rondar ese valor. Un intervalo demasiado estrecho subestima el riesgo; uno demasiado ancho no aporta información. Los gates detectaron problemas reales durante la preparación del ejemplo. Con menos datos y la configuración por defecto, la primera versión registró una transición divergente y una cobertura del 83,6% sobre 67 observaciones de prueba, y fue rechazada. Con más datos y target_accept=0.95 , las siguientes versiones tuvieron cero divergencias y una cobertura del 90,3%. En las pruebas automáticas, una corrida con 500 muestras por cadena quedó por debajo del mínimo de ESS y también fue rechazada. Además de los umbrales, este episodio muestra un detalle: la banda de cobertura tiene que contemplar el tamaño del conjunto de prueba, porque con pocas observaciones la variación es grande. Servir la posterior sin PyMC en runtime serving.py: predictor liviano a partir de muestras guardadas import numpy as np import mlflow class Predictor : def __init__ ( self , a , beta , sigma , seed = 0 ) : self . a , self . beta , self . sigma = a , beta , sigma # (S, T), (S,), (S,) self . rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) @classmethod def desde_idata ( cls , idata , max_draws = 500 , seed = 0 ) : post = idata . posterior . ds . stack ( s = ( "chain" , "draw" ) ) idx = np . linspace ( 0 , post . sizes [ "s" ] - 1 , max_draws ) . astype ( int ) # thinning return cls ( post [ "a" ] . values . T [ idx ] , post [ "beta" ] . values [ idx ] , post [ "sigma" ] . values [ idx ] , seed ) def muestras ( self , tienda , precio ) : mu = self . a [ : , tienda ] + self . beta [ : , None ] * precio [ None , : ] # (S, N) vectorizado return mu + self . sigma [ : , None ] * self . rng . standard_normal ( mu . shape ) class ModeloDemanda ( mlflow . pyfunc . PythonModel ) : def load_context ( self , context ) : d = np . load ( context . artifacts [ "draws" ] ) self . p = Predictor ( d [ "a" ] , d [ "beta" ] , d [ "sigma" ] ) def predict ( self , context , model_input , params = None ) : s = self . p . muestras ( model_input [ "tienda" ] . to_numpy ( ) , model_input [ "precio" ] . to_numpy ( dtype = float ) ) out = model_input . copy ( ) out [ "media" ] = s . mean ( axis = 0 ) out [ "p05" ] , out [ "p95" ] = np . quantile ( s , [ 0.05 , 0.95 ] , axis = 0 ) return out Esta es una de las decisiones de diseño más útiles para modelos bayesianos en producción: separar el ajuste del serving . El ajuste corre con PyMC en un job de entrenamiento; el servicio solo necesita las muestras de los parámetros y una función vectorizada en NumPy que genera la predictiva posterior. Se guardan 500 muestras de las 4.000 disponibles, elegidas a intervalos regulares, y el servicio responde con la media y un intervalo del 90%. En el ejemplo, la latencia p95 para 154 predicciones fue de alrededor de 2 ms. La posterior completa se guarda aparte, en formato NetCDF, para diagnóstico y auditoría. El trade-off es explícito: menos muestras implica menos latencia y más error de Monte Carlo en los cuantiles. Para cuantiles extremos, como un percentil 99 usado en decisiones de stock, 500 muestras pueden no alcanzar. La cantidad debería decidirse con el Data Scientist y quedar registrada como parámetro del modelo. Registrar la versión con su evidencia entrenar.py (fragmento): cada versión queda registrada con métricas y resultado de validación with mlflow . start_run ( ) : mlflow . log_params ( { "draws" : draws , "chains" : 4 , "seed" : seed , "parametrizacion" : "no_centrada" } ) idata = modelo . ajustar ( entreno , draws = draws , seed = seed ) pred = Predictor . desde_idata ( idata ) m = validacion . convergencia ( idata ) m [ "cobertura_90" ] = validacion . cobertura ( pred , tienda_test , precio_test , y_test ) m [ "latencia_p95_ms" ] = validacion . latencia_p95_ms ( pred , tienda_test , precio_test ) mlflow . log_metrics ( m ) fallas = validacion . evaluar ( m ) # ... guardar draws.npz y posterior.nc ... info = mlflow . pyfunc . log_model ( name = "modelo" , python_model = ModeloDemanda ( ) , artifacts = { "draws" : ruta_draws } , code_paths = [ "serving.py" ] , input_example = ejemplo , registered_model_name = NOMBRE ) version = str ( info . registered_model_version ) cliente = mlflow . MlflowClient ( ) cliente . set_model_version_tag ( NOMBRE , version , "validacion" , "rechazada" if fallas else "aprobada" ) cliente . set_model_version_tag ( NOMBRE , version , "validacion.fallas" , "," . join ( fallas ) or "-" ) Registrar también las versiones rechazadas puede parecer innecesario, pero aporta trazabilidad: el historial muestra qué se intentó, por qué no pasó y qué cambió después. La etiqueta validacion es lo que la CLI consulta para permitir o rechazar una promoción. Promoción dev → staging → prod con aliases Las versiones anteriores de MLflow usaban stages fijos (Staging, Production, Archived). Desde la versión 2.9 están deprecados en favor de aliases : nombres mutables que apuntan a una versión, como dev , staging o prod . El servicio carga models:/demanda-tiendas@prod y la promoción consiste en mover el alias. Cuando los entornos están en workspaces o registros separados, como suele ocurrir en organizaciones con requisitos de aislamiento, MlflowClient.copy_model_version copia una versión de un modelo registrado a otro. El principio es el mismo: la versión que llega a producción es exactamente la que se validó, no un reentrenamiento. ml_cli.py (fragmento): ml-deploy verifica los gates antes de mover el alias ENTORNOS = [ "dev" , "staging" , "prod" ] @deploy_app . command ( ) def deploy ( modelo : str , version : str , entorno : str = typer . Option ( . . . , "--to" ) , ticket : str = typer . Option ( "" , help = "Cambio aprobado; obligatorio para prod" ) , dry_run : bool = False ) : """Promueve una versión al entorno indicado si pasa los gates.""" c = MlflowClient ( ) mv = c . get_model_version ( modelo , version ) errores = [ ] if mv . tags . get ( "validacion" ) != "aprobada" : errores . append ( f "validación: {mv.tags.get('validacion', 'sin ejecutar')}" ) previo = ENTORNOS [ ENTORNOS . index ( entorno ) - 1 ] if entorno != "dev" else None if previo and _version_de ( c , modelo , previo ) != str ( version ) : errores . append ( f "la versión {version} no está en {previo}" ) if entorno == "prod" and not ticket : errores . append ( "prod requiere --ticket" ) if errores : typer . echo ( "RECHAZADO: " + "; " . join ( errores ) , err = True ) raise typer . Exit ( code = 2 ) actual = _version_de ( c , modelo , entorno ) typer . echo ( f "{modelo}@{entorno}: {actual or '-'} -> {version}" ) if dry_run : return if actual and actual != str ( version ) : c . set_registered_model_tag ( modelo , f "{entorno}.anterior" , actual ) c . set_registered_model_alias ( modelo , entorno , version ) c . set_model_version_tag ( modelo , version , f "desplegado.{entorno}" , f "{datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()} ticket={ticket or '-'}" ) @rollback_app . command ( ) def rollback ( modelo : str , entorno : str = typer . Option ( . . . , "--env" ) , motivo : str = typer . Option ( . . . ) ) : """Vuelve el alias del entorno a la versión anterior registrada.""" c = MlflowClient ( ) anterior = c . get_registered_model ( modelo ) . tags . get ( f "{entorno}.anterior" ) if not anterior : typer . echo ( f "no hay versión anterior registrada para {entorno}" , err = True ) raise typer . Exit ( code = 2 ) actual = _version_de ( c , modelo , entorno ) c . set_registered_model_alias ( modelo , entorno , anterior ) c . set_registered_model_tag ( modelo , f "{entorno}.anterior" , actual ) c . set_model_version_tag ( modelo , actual , f "revertido.{entorno}" , f "{datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()} motivo={motivo}" ) Las dos funciones se publican como comandos con [project.scripts] en pyproject.toml ( ml-deploy = "ml_cli:deploy_app" y ml-rollback = "ml_cli:rollback_app" ). Una sesión típica se ve así: Salida real de la CLI contra el registro local $ ml-deploy demanda-tiendas 2 --to prod --ticket CHG-9 RECHAZADO: la versión 2 no está en staging $ ml-deploy demanda-tiendas 2 --to dev demanda-tiendas@dev: - - > 2 $ ml-deploy demanda-tiendas 2 --to staging demanda-tiendas@staging: - - > 2 $ ml-deploy demanda-tiendas 2 --to prod --ticket CHG-9 demanda-tiendas@prod: - - > 2 # ... la versión 3 recorre dev y staging ... $ ml-deploy demanda-tiendas 3 --to prod --ticket CHG-10 demanda-tiendas@prod: 2 - > 3 $ ml-rollback demanda-tiendas --env prod --motivo "latencia p95" demanda-tiendas@prod: 3 - > 2 Algunos principios de diseño para estas herramientas: deben ser idempotentes , de modo que repetir un comando no produzca efectos distintos; deben ofrecer --dry-run ; deben dejar evidencia en el registro (quién, cuándo, con qué ticket), y deben devolver códigos de salida distintos para un rechazo por política y para un error técnico, para que el CI pueda tratarlos de forma diferente. El rollback tiene que ser la operación más simple de todas, porque se usa bajo presión. Límites del ejemplo: El ticket se acepta como texto; en una implementación real, la aprobación para prod debería venir de un mecanismo con identidad verificable, como los entornos protegidos con revisores obligatorios de GitHub Actions o GitLab, y la CLI debería ejecutarse desde el pipeline con credenciales de servicio, no desde la laptop de cada persona. El rollback guarda una sola versión anterior; un historial completo es una extensión directa. Suites de testing: qué validar en un modelo bayesiano Las pruebas de un modelo bayesiano combinan las de cualquier software con otras propias del enfoque. Conviene organizarlas por costo, para que las rápidas corran en cada commit y las más caras en la integración o antes de una promoción. Capas de prueba para un modelo bayesiano (propuesta) Prueba Qué detecta Cuándo corre Unitarias y de contrato Errores en transformaciones y en el esquema de entrada y salida Cada commit, segundos Chequeo predictivo a priori Priors que generan valores imposibles, como demandas negativas enormes Cada commit, segundos Recuperación de parámetros Un modelo que no puede recuperar los valores con los que se simularon los datos Cada PR, minutos Diagnósticos de convergencia R-hat alto, ESS bajo, divergencias Cada entrenamiento Calibración y error en holdout Intervalos mal calibrados, peor exactitud que la versión actual Antes de registrar Performance Latencia p95 y memoria fuera del presupuesto Antes de promover La recuperación de parámetros es la prueba más característica: se simulan datos con valores conocidos, se ajusta el modelo y se comprueba que esos valores caen dentro de los intervalos de la posterior. Si un modelo no recupera parámetros de datos que cumplen sus propios supuestos, difícilmente funcione con datos reales. En el ejemplo, la prueba verifica mu_a , beta y sigma dentro del intervalo del 94%. Para una validación más rigurosa del procedimiento de inferencia existe simulation-based calibration , que repite este ejercicio muchas veces; es costosa y suele reservarse para modelos críticos o cambios estructurales. Rendimiento: MCMC, inferencia y MLflow Eficiencia del muestreo La métrica útil no es el tiempo de entrenamiento sino las muestras efectivas por segundo : un muestreador más rápido que produce cadenas muy correlacionadas puede ser peor que uno lento con buena mezcla. Las palancas, en orden aproximado de impacto: reparametrizar el modelo (como la forma no centrada del ejemplo), escalar y centrar predictores, usar priors informativos razonables, y probar otros backends de NUTS. pm.sample acepta nuts_sampler con las opciones pymc , nutpie , numpyro y blackjax ; los dos últimos se basan en JAX y pueden aprovechar GPU. Cuál conviene depende del modelo, así que la plataforma debería facilitar la comparación, por ejemplo registrando ESS por segundo como métrica de cada corrida. Para modelos que se reentrenan con frecuencia y no toleran el costo de MCMC, existen aproximaciones como la inferencia variacional (ADVI) o Pathfinder. Son más rápidas, pero tienden a subestimar la incertidumbre. Si se usan, la validación de calibración se vuelve aún más importante. Velocidad de inferencia Las técnicas principales ya aparecen en el ejemplo: servir desde muestras guardadas en lugar de recompilar el modelo, reducir el número de muestras, vectorizar el cálculo sobre muestras y observaciones a la vez, y cargar el modelo una sola vez al iniciar el servicio. Para cargas por lotes, la predicción se puede ejecutar como job sobre todo el conjunto, con lo que la latencia por solicitud deja de importar. MLflow a escala Con muchos equipos y miles de corridas, MLflow también necesita atención. Un backend en base de datos (PostgreSQL o MySQL) en lugar de archivos locales, con la base dimensionada y mantenida como cualquier otra; artifacts en almacenamiento de objetos, con mlflow server --artifacts-destination cuando se quiere que el servidor actúe como proxy y los clientes no necesiten credenciales del bucket; búsquedas con filtros y paginación ( search_model_versions acepta filter_string , max_results y page_token ) en lugar de traer todo; logging asíncrono ( mlflow.config.enable_async_logging() ) para que el entrenamiento no espere al servidor, y caché de las resoluciones de alias en los servicios, con un tiempo de expiración corto, para no consultar el registro en cada solicitud. Serving de modelos complejos Los modelos bayesianos y los ensembles comparten un problema de serving: una predicción implica muchos cálculos que después se resumen. Algunas pautas de arquitectura ayudan a mantenerlo manejable. Separar ajuste, preparación y serving. El ajuste corre como job; un paso intermedio prepara el artefacto de serving (muestras reducidas, componentes precalculados); el servicio solo carga y calcula. Un contrato de salida que incluya incertidumbre. Media e intervalo, no solo un número. Si los consumidores ignoran el intervalo, el modelo pierde su principal ventaja. Ensembles como un solo artefacto versionado. Los modelos que componen un ensemble se registran juntos o con referencias fijas a versiones, nunca a aliases que puedan moverse por separado. Elegir entre online y batch según el uso. Muchas decisiones de negocio, como planificación de stock o precios, funcionan mejor con predicciones calculadas por lotes y guardadas, que con un servicio en línea. Despliegue gradual para cambios relevantes. Un modelo nuevo puede correr en modo sombra junto al actual, comparando predicciones antes de recibir tráfico real. Monitoreo de la salud del modelo Un dashboard de salud de modelos combina métricas de servicio, de calidad y de proceso de entrenamiento. La tabla propone un conjunto mínimo; los umbrales dependen de cada caso. Métricas de salud de un modelo bayesiano en producción (propuesta) Dimensión Métrica Cuándo se conoce Señal de alerta Servicio Latencia p95, tasa de error, throughput En tiempo real Supera el presupuesto acordado Datos Distribución de las variables de entrada En tiempo real Valores fuera del rango de entrenamiento Exactitud Error absoluto medio, error porcentual Cuando llegan los valores reales Peor que la versión anterior o que un baseline simple Calibración Cobertura de los intervalos del 50% y del 90% Cuando llegan los valores reales Desvío sostenido respecto de la cobertura nominal Entrenamiento R-hat máximo, ESS mínimo, divergencias, ESS por segundo En cada reentrenamiento Degradación respecto de corridas anteriores Uso Versión activa por entorno, fecha del último reentrenamiento Siempre Modelo sin reentrenar más allá de lo previsto La cobertura en producción es la métrica que más información aporta y la que menos se mide. Si el 90% de las ventas reales cae dentro del intervalo del 90%, el modelo cuantifica bien su incertidumbre. Si cae el 70%, el modelo es demasiado confiado y las decisiones que usan el intervalo, como el stock de seguridad, están subestimando el riesgo, aunque el error de la media sea bueno. Gobernanza automatizada La gobernanza manual, con planillas y reuniones de aprobación, no escala y suele convertirse en un trámite. La alternativa es expresar las políticas como chequeos que se ejecutan en el pipeline y dejan evidencia en el registro. Gates técnicos: validación aprobada, orden de entornos respetado, dependencias sin vulnerabilidades conocidas. Gates de documentación: MODEL_CARD.md con propósito, datos de entrenamiento, limitaciones y responsable; sin él, la versión no se promueve. Gates de linaje: la versión tiene etiquetas con el commit del código, la versión de los datos y la imagen de entrenamiento. Aprobación humana donde aporta: para producción y para modelos que afectan decisiones sobre personas, con revisores definidos por política y no por disponibilidad. Auditoría como subproducto: cada promoción y reversión queda registrada con fecha, autor y motivo, sin que nadie tenga que escribir un informe. El objetivo es que el camino aprobado sea también el más fácil. Si cumplir con la política exige más trabajo que saltearla, la gente encuentra cómo saltearla. Autonomía: documentación, formación y feedback Las herramientas no generan autonomía por sí solas.
